teaser: Rejected by a jury of three, one of them a pharmacist. And another painter secretly worked on it.
review_notes:
Cassatt's 1903 letter to Ambroise Vollard (rejection from the American section of the 1878 Exposition Universelle, jury of three including a pharmacist, Degas working on the background, the girl being the child of friends of Degas): paraphrased, check.
Infrared study at the National Gallery of Art (2014) showing the background was changed from a straight wall to a diagonal corner, attributed to Degas: check wording.
Dog identified as a Brussels griffon, a breed Cassatt owned: check.
Shown at the fourth Impressionist exhibition in 1879: check.
Cassatt's later refusal of juries and prizes (e.g. declining an award in 1904): check.
Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon to the National Gallery, 1983: check.

lesson.text: Three. That is how many men sat on the jury that turned this painting down in 1878. Mary Cassatt had sent it to the American section of the World's Fair in Paris. Twenty-five years later she was still angry about it, and she remembered one detail with special bitterness: one of the three judges was a pharmacist.

What did they see that displeased them? A little girl, perhaps five or six, slumped in a huge armchair. Her dress is fresh and her socks match her tartan sash, so someone has dressed her up. But she is not behaving. This is not how children were supposed to appear in a painting.

lesson.title: The art of slouching
lesson.text: In 1878, painted children sat up straight. This one does not.

spots.title: The arm
spots.text: One arm is thrown back behind her head, the gesture of someone who has given up on the afternoon.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Eyes lowered, mouth closed, cheeks flushed. She is not posing for us and not looking at anything in particular. This is plain boredom, painted without mockery.

spots.title: The legs
spots.text: Knees apart, skirt riding up, feet dangling well above the floor. The chair is much too big for her, and she has slid halfway down it.

lesson.text: Portraits of children were usually made to please parents: clean, sweet, well behaved. Cassatt shows what a child actually does when adults stop paying attention. She was 34, an American newly settled in Paris, and she had just been invited by Edgar Degas to join the painters we now call the Impressionists.
The model was the daughter of friends of Degas. Cassatt later recalled that he liked the picture, gave her advice, and even picked up a brush and worked on the background himself.
The girl is not alone in the room. She has a companion who has reached the same conclusion about this afternoon, and who has gone one step further. Scan the other chairs.
Someone else is in this room, fast asleep. Where?

spots.title: The dog
spots.text: A small dark dog curled on the neighboring armchair, eyes shut. It is a Brussels griffon, a breed Cassatt herself kept for much of her life. Girl and dog mirror each other across the room.

lesson.text: The dog matters for the composition too. Its dark coat on the left answers the girl's dark hair and sash on the right. Between them stretches an odd, empty shape of grey-brown floor, with the four pieces of furniture pushed around it like islands.

That empty floor was unusual. A traditional painter would have put the child in the middle and filled the room around her. Cassatt cuts the furniture off at the edges and leaves the center bare, the way a snapshot might, or one of the Japanese prints that Paris artists were collecting.

In 2014, conservators at the National Gallery of Art examined the canvas with infrared light, which can see through the upper layers of paint. They found that the far wall had first been painted as a simple straight line. It was reworked into a corner seen at an angle, which makes the room feel deeper. The change fits what Cassatt said about Degas's help.
A portrait does not have to flatter. By painting a bored child truthfully, Cassatt treated childhood as a real state of mind, not a decoration.

Then there is the blue. It covers nearly half the canvas, and from far away it reads as one color. Come closer and it breaks into dashes of pink, green, orange and white, laid on fast. The upholstery pattern is not drawn, it is suggested by flicks of the brush.
The rest of the picture is yours to wander. Compare how tightly the face is painted with how loosely the chairs are, and see how few strokes it takes to make a shoe buckle shine.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: The most carefully finished part of the painting: smooth skin, pink cheeks, a small shadow under the lip.

spots.title: The tartan
spots.text: The sash is a tangle of dark green, blue, red and yellow strokes. Up close it is nearly abstract; from a distance it becomes plaid.

spots.title: The buckle
spots.text: A few touches of white on black are enough to make a polished buckle catch the light.

spots.title: The sleeping dog
spots.text: Brown muzzle, closed eyes, body sunk into the cushion. The fur is a soft dark mass with almost no detail.

spots.title: The windows
spots.text: Pale panes painted in quick whites and greys. This is the only source of daylight, and it sits behind the girl.

spots.title: The far wall
spots.text: This strip of background, with its light doorway and receding line, is the zone that was reworked to open up the room.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: “Mary Cassatt,” in dark paint on the blue fabric at the lower left.

lesson.text: After the World's Fair rejection, Cassatt showed the painting in 1879 with the Impressionists, who needed no jury's permission. She kept it for years. It is now at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, a gift of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon.
Cassatt never forgave juries. From then on she refused to submit her work to them and later declined prizes too, saying that artists should be free to show without judges.

One question the painting leaves open: what is the girl waiting for? A visit to end, a sitting to finish, permission to go and play? Cassatt gives no clue. Perhaps that is why the picture feels so familiar. Everyone has been that child in that chair.

quiz.question: How many people sat on the jury that rejected the painting in 1878?
quiz.explanation: Three jurors, one of whom was a pharmacist, according to Cassatt.

quiz.question: Which painter helped Cassatt with the background?
quiz.explanation: Degas advised her and worked on the background himself.

quiz.question: What is sleeping on the armchair at the left?
quiz.explanation: A Brussels griffon, a breed Cassatt owned.

quiz.question: What did infrared examination reveal in 2014?
options: The far wall was changed from a straight line to an angled corner
quiz.explanation: The reworked background makes the room feel deeper.

quiz.question: What was unusual about the girl for a child's portrait of the time?
options: She is slouching and visibly bored
She is dressed as an adult
quiz.explanation: Children were normally shown sitting properly and looking sweet.

quiz.question: Where did Cassatt show the painting after its rejection?
quiz.explanation: The Impressionists exhibited without a jury.

facts.text: One of the jurors who rejected the painting was a pharmacist.
facts.explanation: Cassatt recalled this detail with irritation decades later.

facts.text: The blue of the armchairs is painted as one flat, even color.
facts.explanation: It is made of quick dashes of pink, green, orange and white over blue.

facts.text: The girl was the daughter of friends of Degas.
facts.explanation: Cassatt said so herself when she looked back on the picture.
